title: Streaming and perceived latency
summary: Streaming sends tokens to the client as they are generated. Total time does not change, but the first word appears sooner and long calls stop timing out.
useIf: A person reads the answer as it arrives and the answer is longer than a sentence or two.
avoidIf: A program consumes the whole answer, or a check must see the full text before anyone may display it.

explain.md: With `stream: true` the server returns the answer as a series of small events instead of one body. Streaming does not change total time. It lowers the time to the first visible response and avoids client timeouts on long outputs [[r14]]. Perceived latency tracks TTFT, not TTLT, so a 12 second answer that starts in 700 ms feels fast.

explain.title: One streamed call
explain.alt: The client posts a request, the server sends a series of data events, then a completed event.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  C->>S: POST with stream true
  S-->>C: data: delta 1
  S-->>C: data: delta 2
  S-->>C: data: delta n
  S-->>C: completed event

explain.md: Most APIs use **server-sent events** (SSE). The response type is `text/event-stream`, each event is one or more `data:` lines ended by a blank line, `id:` and `retry:` support reconnection through the `Last-Event-ID` header, and a line starting with `:` is a comment. Servers can send a comment about every 15 seconds so that legacy proxies do not drop an idle connection [[tr3]]. On the Responses API the events to handle are `response.created`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.completed` and `error`; Chat Completions puts text in a `delta` field [[tr5]].

explain.text: UI patterns that make it feel fast

items: Show a status line while retrieval or tools run (searching, reading, writing), then switch to text
Render incrementally, batched to animation frames, and keep the scroll position stable
Offer a stop button that cancels the request, so the server stops spending tokens
Show sources or tool results as they arrive, ahead of the final prose

explain.md: **When streaming hurts.** Streaming makes moderation harder, because partial completions are hard to evaluate and moderation scores arrive only after the full output [[tr5]]. A structured output cannot be validated until it is complete. Buffering proxies hold events until the end, and a gateway needs long-lived unbuffered connections [[tr13]]. Token limits cannot count streamed tokens exactly, so APIM `llm-token-limit` always estimates when streaming [[tr14]]. Once text is on screen you cannot silently retry or retract it.

whereToUse: Chat and copilot UIs where users read as text appears
Long outputs (reports, code, explanations) that would otherwise risk client or gateway timeouts
Agent UIs that show progress: tool calls, retrieved sources, partial plans
Voice or text-to-speech pipelines that start speaking on the first sentence
Server-to-server calls where an idle-timeout would otherwise kill a long non-streamed request

use: A human reads the output and TTFT is the felt delay
Answers are long enough that TTLT exceeds a few seconds
You can handle events in the client and the whole path allows unbuffered responses
avoid: A downstream program needs complete, validated JSON before any step may start
Policy requires a full-text safety check before display, and a chunk-level check is not acceptable
A proxy or CDN buffers the response and you cannot change it
flips: Output guard needs the whole answer: stream a status line, then release the text after the check, or guard in sentence-sized chunks
A job only needs to avoid an idle timeout: stream to a server-side buffer and never show partial text
Network is unreliable: add event ids and a resume path, or use background runs and polling

pitfalls.symptom: Nothing appears until the answer completes
pitfalls.cause: A proxy, CDN or gateway buffers the response
pitfalls.fix: Disable response buffering on the path, flush each event, and test through the real route [[tr13]]

pitfalls.symptom: Streamed text could not be filtered before users saw it
pitfalls.cause: Moderation ran on the full output after display
pitfalls.fix: Check in chunks before release, or hold text for high-risk flows [[tr5]]

pitfalls.symptom: Token metrics or limits are off for streamed calls
pitfalls.cause: Gateways estimate streamed tokens, and some OpenAI models need `include_usage: true` for accurate counts
pitfalls.fix: Request usage in the stream where supported and reconcile gateway counts with provider usage [[tr19]]

scenarios.title: Public chat with a safety policy
scenarios.situation: A consumer assistant answers questions for the public. Policy says unsafe text must never be displayed. Typical answers run 400 tokens. Users already complain about the wait.
constraints: High risk of harm if shown
Answers take about 8 seconds in full
unknowns: Can a check run per sentence in under 100 ms?
Is a 1 to 2 second hold on the first sentence acceptable?
scenarios.question: How do you deliver the answer?

options.name: Stream through a chunk-level guard that releases each checked sentence
options.why: Users see the first sentence soon and nothing unchecked is shown.
options.tradeoff: TTFT rises by one chunk plus guard time, and a late unsafe sentence must end the stream.

options.name: Stream raw tokens and moderate afterwards
options.why: Unsafe text is already visible when the check finishes.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for an internal tool with low harm potential.

options.name: Do not stream and check the full answer
options.why: It is the safest, with one simple check.
options.tradeoff: Users wait the full 8 seconds and may leave.

flips.if: The audience is internal staff and the harm potential is low
flips.then: Stream raw and log for review.

flips.if: Guard latency per chunk exceeds the gap between chunks
flips.then: Hold the full answer, show a status line and release after the check.

scenarios.takeaway: Streaming and moderation can coexist when the check works on chunks.

scenarios.title: Extraction job behind a gateway
scenarios.situation: A service extracts a long JSON object from a document and passes it to an order system. No human watches. Calls sometimes take 90 seconds and the gateway closes idle connections at 60 seconds.
unknowns: Can the gateway timeout be raised?
Is the call idempotent if retried?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Stream, accumulate on the server, validate, then pass on
options.why: Bytes flow, so the idle timeout does not fire, and the consumer still sees only complete JSON.
options.tradeoff: No latency gain for the end consumer, plus a little event handling code.

options.name: Stream partial JSON to the order system
options.why: The downstream step would act on incomplete data.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable only for a consumer that parses incrementally and tolerates partial objects.

options.name: Keep the non-streamed call and retry on timeout
options.why: It is simple and works if calls are idempotent.
options.tradeoff: Each retry repeats the full cost and delay.

flips.if: The timeout can be raised above worst-case latency
flips.then: A plain non-streamed call is the simplest choice.
Use background mode and poll for the result.

scenarios.takeaway: Streaming also fixes timeouts, even when no one reads the partial text.

quiz.q: What does turning on streaming change for a 10 second answer?
options: Total generation time drops by half
The first words appear sooner, but total generation time is about the same
Output tokens are billed at a lower rate
The model skips the prefill phase
quiz.explain: Streaming lowers time to first response and avoids client timeouts, but it does not change total time. Billing and prefill are unaffected.

quiz.q: Which situations make streaming a poor fit?
options: A program must validate a full JSON object before use
A response buffering proxy sits in the path and cannot be changed
A person reads a long answer in a chat window
Users want a stop button to cancel generation
quiz.explain: Full-object validation and unbuffered delivery are the two blockers. A human reading and a stop button are reasons to stream.

quiz.q: Match each SSE element to its role.

pairs.r: Sets the Last-Event-ID sent on reconnect
Sets the reconnection time in milliseconds

quiz.explain: These are the four stream elements defined in the HTML living standard. The colon comment is what servers send about every 15 seconds to keep legacy proxies from dropping the connection.

flashcards.front: What does streaming change and not change?
flashcards.back: It lowers time to the first visible token and avoids client timeouts. Total generation time stays about the same.

flashcards.front: Name two reasons streaming can hurt.
flashcards.back: Moderation of partial text is harder, and full-object validation or buffering proxies defeat it.

flashcards.front: What keeps an SSE connection alive through legacy proxies?
flashcards.back: A comment line (starting with a colon) sent about every 15 seconds.
